name: Barry Whitfield
presenting_complaint: Visible (macroscopic) haematuria with lower urinary tract symptoms

medical_history.social: Ex-smoker, 30 pack-years, quit 5 years ago. Former carpenter with historical occupational exposure to industrial dyes and rubber solvents. Social alcohol.
medical_history.family: Father died of a bladder problem.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: Barry Whitfield, a 68-year-old male ex-smoker, presents with one week of visible red/pink urine, most times he voids, with a couple of small clots and no pain. He also reports several months of nocturia, weak stream, terminal dribbling, urgency and incomplete emptying. He is haemodynamically stable and frightened it may be cancer. DRE shows a smooth, non-nodular, enlarged prostate.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Characterise haematuria: timing in the stream (total/initial/terminal), presence of clots, painless vs painful, duration
Malignancy risk screen: smoking history, occupational aniline dye/rubber/hydrocarbon exposure, prior pelvic radiotherapy or cyclophosphamide, schistosomiasis travel
Quantify and group LUTS into voiding/obstructive vs storage/irritative (consider IPSS)
Constitutional/red-flag screen: weight loss, bone or back pain, appetite; family history of urological cancer
Exclude mimics: infection (dysuria/fever), stones, recent heavy exercise/trauma, beetroot/dye ingestion, glomerulonephritis (recent sore throat)
Anticoagulant/antiplatelet use (on aspirin) - never let this be the reason to skip investigation
objective: Abdominal exam for palpable bladder (retention) and flank/renal masses or tenderness
Digital rectal examination: document prostate size, consistency, nodularity (smooth non-nodular here)
Urine dipstick and formal microscopy to confirm true haematuria (RBCs present, not myoglobin/pseudohaematuria)
Vital signs and assessment for anaemia/clot retention
assessment: Visible (macroscopic) haematuria in a man over 40 - urothelial/bladder cancer until proven otherwise
BPH is a diagnosis of exclusion for haematuria - a smooth, benign-feeling prostate does NOT explain or exclude a bladder tumour
Differential: bladder/urothelial cancer, renal cell carcinoma, prostate cancer, urinary calculi, UTI, glomerulonephritis, BPH, pseudohaematuria
plan: Urgent urology referral for flexible cystoscopy PLUS upper-tract imaging with CT urography - regardless of the benign DRE
Urine microscopy, culture and sensitivities, and urine cytology
Bloods: FBC, UEC/eGFR, coagulation profile (on aspirin), PSA (after counselling)
Do NOT attribute the bleeding to BPH and discharge, and do not falsely reassure that a smooth prostate explains the blood
Address the patient's cancer fear honestly without false reassurance; explain plan in plain language and safety-net
Defer any alpha-blocker/5-alpha-reductase treatment for BPH until malignancy is excluded

critical_errors: Attributing the visible haematuria to BPH because the prostate feels benign, and failing to arrange flexible cystoscopy plus CT urography
Blaming the bleeding on aspirin and skipping malignancy investigation
Falsely reassuring the patient and discharging without a haematuria work-up in a man over 40
must_not_miss: Bladder/urothelial cancer work-up (cystoscopy + CT urography) initiated
Upper urinary tract malignancy (renal cell carcinoma) considered
No false reassurance that a benign prostate explains macroscopic haematuria
